summary: First English narrative for Masao Yoshida's decision on 12 March 2011 to keep injecting seawater into Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1 after TEPCO's head office decided to suspend it, written from the case's verified facts (INPO 11-005; NAIIC executive summary; The Japan Times, 27 May 2011). The disputed origin of the stop instruction is left unresolved.

narrative.hook: Twenty minutes ago your workers finally got seawater flowing into a reactor that has had no power for more than a day. Now head office in Tokyo says stop. You run the plant. Do you obey?
narrative.short_setup: It is the evening of 12 March 2011 at TEPCO's Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station, the day after the earthquake and tsunami. Unit 1 lost all electricity when the tsunami hit. Since early morning, workers have kept freshwater flowing into the reactor from the fire-protection system, but by mid-afternoon the tank was running out, and the site superintendent, Masao Yoshida, directed that seawater be used instead. At 15:36 a hydrogen explosion tore open the Unit 1 reactor building. It injured five workers, scattered highly radioactive debris, wrecked the hoses and fire engines laid out for seawater, and stopped all injection into the core. By 18:25 the government had widened the evacuation zone to 20 km. At 19:04, after hours of work in those conditions, a fire engine began pumping seawater into the reactor. Then head office decided to suspend it. By TEPCO's later account, the government's approval for seawater had not yet been obtained, and in Tokyo the question of whether seawater could restart a chain reaction was being discussed.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: In a nuclear emergency the chain of command is not a formality. The plant was one part of a response that involved TEPCO's head office, the regulators and the government, and decisions taken by the site alone could leave everyone else working from the wrong picture. Head office had a stated reason: government approval for seawater had not yet been given. A concern about re-criticality had been raised in Tokyo, and the site was in no position to rule it out on its own. Pausing until approval came meant respecting the people who carried national responsibility for the accident, at the cost of what might be only a short delay.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: From the plant, the danger looked immediate and certain. Unit 1 had gone without cooling through the afternoon after the explosion, and injection had only just been restored after hours of dangerous work. Stopping meant the core would again get no water, for however long it took Tokyo to decide, and restarting might not be quick. The worry about re-criticality was real enough to be discussed, but it was a possibility, not a known effect, and boron could be added to the water. To the site, keeping water flowing was the single most important thing it could do to stop the accident getting worse.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: Yoshida kept the seawater flowing. Head office did not know. It was only after TEPCO held hearings with workers at the plant in May that the company learned what had happened. On 26 May 2011 TEPCO vice president Sakae Muto said that the plant director had judged water injection to be the most important measure for preventing the accident from spreading, and that the injection had in fact continued without a temporary suspension. Muto said the utility had decided on its own to halt the injection because it had not yet obtained the government's approval. Yoshida's own account of how the instruction was handled is not used here.
narrative.outcome_story: Seawater injection into Unit 1 continued, with boron added to address concerns about criticality, and off-site power was restored to the unit on 20 March. TEPCO's later analysis indicated that core damage in Unit 1 had begun at about 18:50 on 11 March, a full day before the order to stop. The public record took two months to catch up. On 21 May TEPCO announced that the injection had been halted for about 55 minutes from 19:25; five days later it reversed itself, and the chief cabinet secretary rebuked the company for the flip-flop. By then the question of who had ordered the stop had become political. Media reports had said the Prime Minister ordered it; Prime Minister Naoto Kan denied that either the Prime Minister or the government had given such an order. Before the Diet's investigation commission, Kan later said that the instruction might have come from TEPCO staff who were at the Prime Minister's Office. That commission found that the Prime Minister's Office, unaware of what TEPCO and the regulators had agreed on venting and seawater injection, had intervened and added to the confusion.
narrative.hindsight_analysis:
It is tempting to tell this as the story of a brave plant manager who ignored the bureaucrats and was proven right. The record supports something more careful.

On decision quality, the choice to keep injecting rates as reasonable. Its technical logic was strong. The reactor had been without cooling for hours, injection had just been restored, and a stop would have reopened the gap for an unknown time. The fear of re-criticality was real enough to be raised, but by the Diet commission's later account the chair of the Nuclear Safety Commission had called the possibility only 'not zero'. Against this stands the cost of how it was done. The site overrode head office during a national emergency, and head office and the government were left believing the injection had stopped. That false picture lasted two months and became part of the public record. A plant that cannot be relied on to report what it is doing is harder to coordinate in the next crisis. The rating is reasonable rather than strong for that reason.

On outcome quality, the result is mixed and hard to measure. Cooling was not interrupted, and no one has shown that continuing caused harm. But TEPCO's own analysis placed the start of Unit 1's core damage on the previous evening, so continuous injection on 12 March could not undo what had already happened. Whether it limited later damage or releases is not settled by the sources used here. The episode also left behind a public dispute about who ordered the stop, which the sources do not resolve. Early reports pointed to the Prime Minister; Kan denied it; TEPCO said it acted on its own.

The fair verdict: a sound technical judgment, made under extreme pressure, that kept water on the core at the price of breaking the chain of information that everyone else depended on.
narrative.decision_principle: When the person closest to the danger is told to stop an action they judge essential, the strongest course is often to keep doing it and say so openly; defying an instruction quietly may protect the immediate situation but leaves everyone else making decisions on a false picture.
narrative.longform_story:
On the afternoon of 11 March 2011, a huge earthquake struck off the coast of north-eastern Japan, and the tsunami that followed swept over the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station. Unit 1 lost all electricity. Without power, there was no ordinary way to keep cooling water flowing over the nuclear fuel.

The plant's workers improvised. From 5:46 on the morning of 12 March they injected freshwater into the reactor from the fire-protection system. At about 14:30 they managed to vent the containment to relieve pressure. But the freshwater would not last. By 14:53 the fire-protection tank was running out, and the site superintendent, Masao Yoshida, ordered the plant's workers to prepare to inject seawater.

At 15:36 hydrogen that had leaked from the damaged reactor exploded inside the Unit 1 building. The blast tore the building open, injured five workers and threw highly radioactive debris across the site. It also destroyed much of what the workers had just laid out: cables, generators, fire engines, and the hoses meant for seawater. All injection into the core stopped. By 18:25 the government had extended the evacuation zone around the plant to 20 kilometres.

The workers started again. At 19:04 a fire engine began pumping seawater through the core spray system into the reactor. After a day without power and an afternoon without any cooling at all, water was reaching Unit 1 again.

Then head office in Tokyo decided to stop it. According to TEPCO's later account, the reason was that the government had not yet approved seawater injection. In Tokyo, people had been discussing whether seawater could make the damaged fuel go critical again and restart a chain reaction. Kan later told the Diet's commission that the chair of the Nuclear Safety Commission had indicated the possibility was not zero.

This was the moment Yoshida faced. The case for obeying was more than habit. A nuclear emergency on this scale involved the company, the regulators and the government. If every site manager acted on their own judgment, no one in Tokyo could know what was really happening at the plant. Head office had a reason, the government had not yet decided, and a pause might be short.

The case for continuing came from what Yoshida could see. The reactor had already gone hours without water. The plant's workers had just restarted injection under brutal conditions. Stopping would leave the core dry again for as long as it took Tokyo to make up its mind, and there was no guarantee the pumping could be restarted quickly. The danger of re-criticality was a possibility under discussion. The danger of no cooling was certain.

Yoshida kept the seawater flowing. Head office was not told. For two months TEPCO's public account said the opposite. On 21 May the company announced that injection into Unit 1 had stopped at 19:25 on 12 March and resumed about 55 minutes later, based on notes and statements from its officials in Tokyo. Only after it began hearings with workers at the plant did it learn otherwise. On 26 May TEPCO vice president Sakae Muto told reporters that the plant director had decided water injection was the most important measure for preventing the accident from spreading, and that it had never actually stopped. The government's chief cabinet secretary, Yukio Edano, rebuked the company. TEPCO, Edano said, needed to grasp the facts accurately and report them.

By then the order itself had become a political fight. Media reports had said Prime Minister Naoto Kan ordered the stop over fears of re-criticality. Kan denied it completely. TEPCO said it had decided on its own because it lacked government approval. Later, before the Diet's independent investigation commission, Kan said that although the decision had been reported as coming from the Prime Minister's Office, it could have been a statement by TEPCO staff who were there at the time. The commission found that the Prime Minister's Office, not knowing what TEPCO and the regulators had already agreed about venting and seawater injection, had intervened and added to the confusion. Who exactly said 'stop' remains disputed.

What difference did Yoshida's choice make? Less, perhaps, than the legend suggests. TEPCO's later analysis found that core damage in Unit 1 had begun at about 18:50 on 11 March, a full day before the order to stop. Continuous injection on 12 March could not reverse that. The seawater, with boron added to address criticality concerns, kept flowing in the days that followed, and off-site power reached Unit 1 again on 20 March. Whether those uninterrupted minutes on 12 March limited later damage is not something these sources can settle.

What the case does show is the shape of a hard choice. Yoshida's technical judgment was sound: in a reactor without cooling, water mattered more than permission. But the way it was carried out, by continuing without telling head office, meant that the people coordinating the national response were working from a false picture, and the public record stayed wrong for two months. The decision kept water on the core. It also broke the line of information that a crisis response depends on. Both are part of the story.
